meta.title: How This System Was Designed — Technical Considerations

scenes.title: What kind of problem this is
scenes.narration: This is an admissions system, and the thing that makes it hard isn't any one screen. One patient is handled by six roles in turn — the ED, the specialists, bed management, the ward nurse, housekeeping. No single one of them owns whether the outcome is correct. Correctness comes from how they hand off to each other. So that's what I designed for.

scenes.title: The domain, as a data model
scenes.narration: Here's the model. Five entities in a tree: a level holds wards, a ward holds beds. A bed is always in exactly one of four states. Six roles act on it, each with its own view. And it needs to talk to three outside systems — patient records, sister hospitals, notifications — none of which I have access to. That last line is the constraint that shapes every decision after this.

scenes.title: 02b-bed-board-capture
scenes.narration: This is the bed board. It looks like a dashboard, but it's a state machine. Every action is a legal move from one state to the next, and a bed can't leave a state without entering another. That's the first correctness property: a bed can never quietly go missing.

scenes.title: The two easy ways to build this both fail
scenes.narration: There are two easy ways to build a prototype like this, and both fail. One: fake everything behind a nice UI. On camera, a real safety rule and a fake one look the same, so it proves nothing. Two: build all of it for real. That doesn't finish — no records endpoint, no identity provider, no solver licence, one engineer, no production access. So the real decision is where to spend the effort I did have.

scenes.title: No bed until every consult is in
scenes.narration: First decision. A patient who needs specialist input is not put in the bed queue right away. The request is held, hidden from bed management, until every consult comes back. Only when all of them are complete does it become eligible for a bed. The trade-off is that entry is slower. But the alternative — allocating a bed before the specialists agree — means placing a patient the assessment might still change. In this domain that's the wrong trade.

scenes.title: 05a-consult-hold-capture
scenes.narration: You can see the rule stated in the ED view. When the doctor picks a patient and sends the case to specialist clusters, the admission is held in ASSESSMENT_PENDING. It won't reach bed management until the consults resolve. This is the gate, in the UI, on the way in.

scenes.title: 05b-consensus-gate-terminal
scenes.narration: And it holds even when the consults come back one at a time. This test completes some of the broadcasts but not all, and checks the request is still held. Partial agreement is not agreement. The bed queue only sees it once the last consult lands.

scenes.title: When specialists disagree, the system takes the safe side
scenes.narration: Second decision. Multiple specialists can review the same patient, and they can disagree — different acuity, different monitoring. The system doesn't ask a coordinator to settle it. It takes the highest acuity anyone assigned, and it turns on every monitoring requirement anyone flagged. The cost is that it sometimes provisions more than a patient strictly needs. In exchange, a disagreement can never resolve toward the less safe option. That's deliberate.

scenes.title: 06a-discordance-terminal
scenes.narration: This is that rule as code. When the consults are reconciled, the effective acuity is set to the highest one across all respondents, and the queue sorts on that effective tier — not on the ED's original number. The test pins it: give it a higher specialist tier, and the effective tier moves up.

scenes.title: Who decides the clinical picture and who decides the bed are different people
scenes.narration: Third decision, and it's about who decides what. Clinicians decide the clinical picture — acuity, monitoring, whether to divert. They don't touch the ward or the bed. That's bed management's call, after consensus. I split it because making doctors negotiate a ward in the middle of emergency triage creates friction between departments and pulls them off patient care. The cost is one more handoff. The benefit is that each call is made by the person who should own it, with the information they actually have.

scenes.title: 07a-admitting-authority-capture
scenes.narration: You can see the split on the queue. The blue badge is the admitting cluster the coordinator set — that's the authoritative one. The plain badge is the ED's suspected service. The allocation engine scores against the coordinator's choice, not the ED's guess. Two different decisions, two different owners, and the system knows which one is authoritative.

scenes.title: Two people can race for the same thing; only one wins
scenes.narration: Fourth decision, about concurrency. Two specialists can try to claim the same case, and two coordinators can try to allocate the same bed. Only one can win. I used optimistic locking — a version column — not pessimistic locking. The reason is the cost of losing the race. Here, the loser just gets a conflict, sees the case is already taken, and picks the next one. Nothing is lost. Pessimistic locking would hold a database lock to prevent a conflict that costs nothing and fixes itself, and it adds deadlock risk and pool pressure. So optimistic is the correct trade, not just the cheaper one.

cards.text: Pessimistic locking — hold a database lock so a second writer waits.

cards.title: What it does instead
cards.text: Version columns on 3 entities. The losing write gets a 409.
cards.detail: Trade-off — the loser retries, which is free

scenes.title: 08a-vacate-capture
scenes.narration: First, the state machine itself. A nurse discharges a patient, and the bed doesn't go straight to available — it goes to pending cleaning, with a thirty-minute clock. There's no jump from occupied to clean, because in a real hospital there isn't one.

scenes.title: 08a2-sanitise-capture
scenes.narration: Housekeeping signs off the cleaning, and only then does the bed return to the pool as clean. Four states, three gates, one owner for each move. Every transition goes through one service method, so there's a single place the write happens — which is what makes the version check enough.

scenes.title: 08b-conflict-409-terminal
scenes.narration: The race itself I can't show honestly in a browser — a real race needs two clients at once, and faking it in one tab would be a lie. So it's a test. Two specialists claim the same broadcast: the first write wins, the second comes back as a 409 Conflict with a problem-detail body the client can act on. That's the loser retrying, which costs nothing.

scenes.title: Provable where built, loud where not
scenes.narration: Fifth decision, about proof. Every operational metric can be computed two ways — from the database and from the audit log — and a test fails if the two disagree. And for the parts I didn't build: they sit behind interfaces chosen by a Spring profile, and the production versions throw the moment they're called instead of returning fake data. The honest cost is that only the prototype side of each boundary is actually tested. But an unbuilt piece that fails loudly is safer than one that quietly pretends.

scenes.title: 09a-analytics-capture
scenes.narration: This is the database pathway. Twenty metrics across four sections, each with a benchmark and how it scored. These are numbers the running system produced from the workflows in this walkthrough — not figures on a slide.

scenes.title: 09b-parity-terminal
scenes.narration: And the two pathways are checked against each other, not eyeballed. The reconciliation test computes each metric both ways and fails if they disagree. That's the only thing that makes a second pathway worth maintaining.

scenes.title: 09c-stub-contract-terminal
scenes.narration: And the stubs are tested to fail. The three production adapters — the solver, the records gateway, the transfer gateway — each throw the moment they're invoked. A placeholder nobody tests eventually gets called by accident, in a profile nobody checked. These can't.

scenes.title: 09d-coverage-capture
scenes.narration: Measured across the whole backend: ninety-four percent of instructions, ninety-seven percent of lines, sixty-nine percent of branches. The branch number is the one worth saying out loud, because that's where the untested paths are. It shows the domain layer is well exercised. It is not a quality gate.

scenes.title: 09e-gate-red-terminal
scenes.narration: And here's the most honest thing I can show you. The frontend declares four coverage thresholds at ninety percent. Run them and one comes back red — branches at seventy-five. Nothing caught it, because nothing runs it automatically. A threshold no pipeline runs isn't a safeguard; it's a number in a config file. That's on the list of what's owed.

scenes.title: What's stubbed, and the boundary it's stubbed behind
scenes.narration: So here's what's stubbed, and it's stubbed on purpose. In-memory data a restart wipes. Polling instead of push. A heuristic instead of a real solver. Header personas instead of real authentication. And no CI to run the coverage gates. Every one of these sits behind an interface or a profile that's already in place, so the production version is added, not retrofitted. On method: AI wrote a lot of this code. Which trade-off to make, which approach was right, and the final shape of the code — those decisions were mine.
